query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys for structural applications, deliberately introducing controlled Cr and oxygen doping followed by tailored thermo‐mechanical processing to achieve a duplex lamellar microstructure with spatially distributed O‐rich clusters will synergistically improve the strength–ductility balance, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance over conventionally processed alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and standard composition lacking targeted Cr enrichment and controlled oxygen incorporation.
generation.intervention: Add controlled amounts of Cr and oxygen to the alloy composition and apply a specifically designed thermo‐mechanical processing route (e.g., casting, rolling, and annealing) to promote phase decomposition into a duplex lamellar structure containing multiple O‐rich clusters.
generation.conditions: This approach is expected to work under processing conditions that allow precise control of doping levels and thermal history. It should hold in structural applications at high temperatures when the microstructural heterogeneity is preserved. It may not work if oxygen levels exceed optimal ranges or if processing conditions fail to produce the desired lamellar structure.
generation.structural_mediator: A duplex lamellar microstructure with evenly distributed O‐rich clusters and stabilized interfacial phases.
generation.mechanism: Higher Cr content is known to enhance local deformation resistance, while the presence of multiple separate O‐rich clusters (linked to Snoek‐type relaxations) provides both a strengthening and damping effect. Together, these microstructural features can improve work hardening and delay crack propagation, thereby leading to increased yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The engineered alloy is predicted to exhibit significant improvements (on the order of approximately 10–20%) in yield strength, ductility, and Young’s modulus, as well as enhanced fracture resistance, relative to standard high-entropy alloys processed without these modifications.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys produced with conventional compositions and processing routes that do not incorporate targeted Cr and oxygen doping or yield duplex lamellar microstructures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is contingent on achieving precise control over doping levels and processing parameters. It may not hold if the processing conditions result in excessive oxidation, non-uniform dopant distribution, or if service conditions cause further microstructural degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements and optimal doping concentrations remain uncertain and will require systematic experimentation. Interactions between Cr and oxygen doping and their influence on the microstructural evolution need further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with the controlled Cr and oxygen doping processed via the tailored thermo‐mechanical route to obtain the duplex lamellar microstructure, and a control set with conventional composition and processing. Conduct a series of mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests to measure yield strength, ductility via % elongation, fracture toughness tests, and dynamic mechanical analysis for Young’s modulus) under identical conditions.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) to verify the presence of duplex lamellar structure and O-rich clusters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 10% increase) in yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance compared to the control samples, or if the targeted duplex lamellar structure with distributed O-rich clusters is not observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. The present work reports the interfacial behaviors and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) based on first-principles calculations. It is found the stability of HEA-reinforced AMCs is strongly dependent on the local chemical compositions in the interfacial regions, i.e., those regions containing more Ni atoms (>25%) or fewer Al atoms (<20%) render more stable interfaces in the HEA-reinforced AMCs. It is calculated that the interfacial energy of Al(001)/Al20Co19Cr19Fe19Ni19(001) interfaces varies from −0.242 eV/Å2 to −0.192 eV/Å2, suggesting that the formation of interfaces at (100) atomic plane is energetically favorable. For those constituent alloy elements presented at the interfaces, Ni could stabilize the interface whereas Al tends to deteriorate the stability of interface. It is determined that although the HEA-reinforced AMCs have less yield strength compared to aluminum, their Young’s modulus is enhanced from 69 GPa for pure Al to 134 GPa.
